q1: Decision: If systemic treatment starts now, use single-agent oral temozolomide on a standard days 1–5 every 28 days schedule, after a CBC and metabolic panel. The only other chemotherapy I would consider, and would not start now, is ifosfamide plus etoposide. Reasons: The diagnosis is still high-grade spindle cell/mesenchymal neoplasm, NOS, not a confirmed glioma, sarcoma, or solitary fibrous tumor (STAT6 negative, no NAB2::STAT6). The 2026-12-12 MRI was one week after 60 Gy and was compared with the pre-operative scan, so it does not reliably prove progression of residual tumor left beside eloquent cortex; that argues against intensive multi-agent chemotherapy, not for an empiric targeted drug. Temozolomide is the appropriate bridge: oral, CNS-penetrant, reversible toxicity, and easy to stop if a real entity or a tissue-confirmed target appears. Ifosfamide/etoposide is the sarcoma regimen I would hold in reserve because both drugs have some CNS activity, but its toxicity is not justified while the entity is open, the plasma result is due, and true progression is unproven. I would not use doxorubicin-based AIM or gemcitabine/docetaxel for intracranial disease because of poor CNS delivery, and I would not use PCV or temozolomide/lomustine, which assume a glioma and a known MGMT status that this patient does not have.
q2: Decision: No. I would not add a second chemotherapy drug. Reasons: Several weeks of good tolerance is not an indication to intensify, and there is no on-treatment response assessment. No doublet has a defined benefit in high-grade spindle cell/mesenchymal neoplasm, NOS, and the entity is still unconfirmed, so a partner drug cannot be chosen rationally: lomustine would assume MGMT-methylated glioma, and etoposide, irinotecan, or ifosfamide would assume a defined sarcoma. Adding any of them now increases myelosuppression and may force a temozolomide dose reduction without a known gain. Continue single-agent temozolomide and change treatment only for documented progression or for a confirmed diagnosis or tissue-confirmed target. Bevacizumab is not chemotherapy and is not indicated by tolerance alone.
q3: Decision: No. I will not stop temozolomide and I will not change to targeted therapy. Reasons: An FGFR2 fusion plus KRAS, STK11, and CTNNB1 on plasma does not establish the histologic entity, and a molecular finding alone must not be treated as if it did. Primary CNS tumors shed little DNA into plasma, so these calls cannot be assumed to come from the frontal mass; they may be clonal hematopoiesis, a separate clone, or assay artifact, and no variant allele fractions are given. The pattern is not a coherent intracranial mesenchymal profile and does not reclassify the resected tumor: FGFR2 fusions and KRAS with STK11 are carcinoma patterns, and CTNNB1 is a WNT alteration seen in unrelated tumors. I would not start pemigatinib, futibatinib, or erdafitinib. FGFR inhibitors are not tumor-agnostic, the fusion partner is unspecified, the call is not confirmed in tumor tissue or by RNA, and concurrent KRAS is a MAPK bypass that makes FGFR blockade unlikely to work even if the fusion were real and in the same clone. The KRAS allele is unspecified, so a G12C inhibitor is not selectable and would be the wrong disease anyway; STK11 and CTNNB1 have no approved drug that should replace chemotherapy, and this pattern is not an indication for immunotherapy. The prior tissue panel found no actionable alteration. Continue temozolomide. Reconsider a matched agent only if the resection specimen confirms a tumor-restricted actionable alteration and shows these plasma variants are not in the tumor.
